title: Orwin
slugLine: An AI-native workflow for software teams that designs the solution, builds the architecture and reviews the code, all on one board.

image.alt: The Orwin board in dark mode: five columns from Backlog to Done, with cards such as a Stripe webhook story marked Passing in Done.

research.problem: As AI makes software development more accessible, the bottleneck is shifting from ==writing code== to **managing the product development process**: requirements, planning, design, development and validation still live in disconnected tools.

stakeholders.name: Teams of 5 to 500 developers
stakeholders.note: Where a unified SDLC pitch resonates most

stakeholders.name: Coding agents and editors
stakeholders.note: Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, VS Code

painPoints.label: Context drift
painPoints.detail: The agent changes one part of the system without seeing the full design and breaks behaviour elsewhere, in code nobody touched.

painPoints.label: Fragmentation
painPoints.detail: New code ignores existing conventions and services, so logic lands in the wrong layer and duplicates what is already there.

painPoints.label: Prompt churn
painPoints.detail: Without a written spec, developers correct the agent prompt after prompt, burning tokens and time, and none of that context is saved.

painPoints.label: Negative hallucination
painPoints.detail: The agent silently leaves out a requirement or edge case and the code still passes its tests, because the tests check what was built, not what was asked for.

painPoints.label: Security gaps
painPoints.detail: Hardcoded secrets, missing access checks and dependencies with known CVEs reach the codebase unscanned.

painPoints.label: No reuse
painPoints.detail: Architecture and components from past projects are designed and built again instead of reused.

headlines.headline: of AI-generated code had an OWASP Top 10 vulnerability

insights.evidence: Pre-implementation analysis and requirements challenge are unclaimed by every competitor in 2026. They are the quality gate that currently lives nowhere, and that is the wedge.

insights.insight: Atlassian is the most dangerous competitor
insights.evidence: Rovo Agents describe an agentic SDLC from PRD to Jira epic, a pitch nearly identical to Orwin’s. But Atlassian’s execution is slow and its UX is legacy.

insights.insight: Copilot and Cursor are partners, not enemies
insights.evidence: Both need a context layer to feed their agents. Orwin’s MCP server turns them into its main distribution channel.
Linear has MCP, Atlassian has Rovo and GitHub has Agent HQ. Orwin needs to own the context-layer category before an incumbent captures that story.

design.lead: Requirements, stories, architecture, tests and pull-request reviews live on one board. Orwin drafts each artifact, reviews its own output and waits for approval before moving on, so it takes part at every step, never in another tab.

items.title: Design
items.body: Five design documents, Problem to Requirements, each run past an AI critic. You choose which findings apply.

items.title: Plan
items.body: Epics and stories with acceptance criteria are proposed from the requirements, and you approve each one.

items.title: Architecture
items.body: Services, data flow and the contract at each boundary are agreed once, and every story is built against them.

items.title: Board
items.body: Moving a card starts the work: Testing drafts the test cases, In Review opens the pull request.

items.title: Build
items.body: One command loads a story’s criteria, tests and design into Cursor, Claude Code or VS Code, and the approach is approved before any code is written.

items.title: Test
items.body: Each test case becomes a happy-path, edge and error test, and insufficient coverage blocks the merge.

items.title: Review
items.body: Opening the pull request runs about ten structured checks, acceptance criteria first, each finding citing a file and line.

items.title: Done
items.body: One card carries the work from the first design document to the merged pull request, with a human approval at every gate.

image.alt: Orwin’s design documents screen: the Solution Design document for a billing story, with an open review finding about the idempotency replay window and an applied one about signature checks.
Orwin’s review screen for a pull request: acceptance criteria, security, tests and contracts resolved, a docs suggestion, and one blocking performance finding citing src/webhooks/stripe.ts line 42.

results.lead: Orwin sizes ==a $5.5B serviceable market== of development teams with 5 to 500 developers, priced at about $100 a seat a month.
